extracted.intended_audience: manufacturers/importers/classifiers of chemicals; safety/compliance officers and hazard communication professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria and explanatory guidance from OSHA's final rule discussion updating Appendix A (hazard classification) to align with GHS Rev. 7/8, covering definitions, tiered evaluation, classification criteria for skin/eye hazards, mixtures, test methods, and related procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopted health hazard definitions (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA is finalizing revised health hazard definitions from Rev. 7 that are more general and neutral with respect to test guidelines; definitions should be clear and concise and test guideline criteria should not be part of a definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA moved test guideline references out of definitions into paragraphs outlining classification criteria. The finalized list of definitions includes acute toxicity; skin corrosion; skin irritation; serious eye damage; eye irritation; respiratory sensitization; skin sensitization; germ cell mutagenicity; carcinogenicity; reproductive toxicity; STOT-SE; STOT-RE; aspiration hazard; and aspiration. OSHA explains the rationale: definitions should differentiate from 'general considerations' text and not embed testing criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin corrosion definition
rubrics_metrics.description: “Skin corrosion refers to the production of irreversible damage to the skin; namely, visible necrosis through the epidermis and into the dermis occurring after initial exposure to a substance or mixture.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA added the word “initial” to clarify the temporal parameter. Definitions are aligned with GHS Rev. 7/8. Classification decisions should use the tiered approach and validated test methods as described elsewhere in Appendix A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin irritation definition
rubrics_metrics.description: “Skin irritation refers to the production of reversible damage to the skin occurring after initial exposure to a substance or mixture.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA added 'initial' to the definition. For classification, paragraph A.2.2.2.1 (now A.2.2.2.2.1) includes language “following its application for up to 4 hours” drawn from GHS/OECD test guidelines; OSHA maintained GHS-consistent wording and clarified one-time exposure through related language additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-parameter wording for skin irritation tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of GHS/OECD-consistent phrasing such as “for up to 4 hours” and addition of wording specifying 'initial' or 'when after the first application' to indicate one-time exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA retained the GHS language (“for up to 4 hours”) because classifiers are familiar with it; to address concerns about implying continuous application, OSHA added 'initial' in the definition and the phrase “when after the first application” in A.2.2.2.2.2 to make clear these provisions refer to a one-time exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiered evaluation approach (Figure A.2.1 / A.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification decisions should follow a tiered evaluation scheme (Figure A.2.1 for skin corrosion/irritation; Figure A.3.1 for serious eye damage/eye irritation) that sequences data evaluation (e.g., existing human data, existing animal data, in vitro/ex vivo data, other information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA aligned text with GHS tiered approach (Rev. 7/8). The agency emphasizes that all available and relevant information must be considered and that classifiers should use weight-of-evidence decisions. Figures and paragraphs were updated to clarify Steps 1a/1b/1c and the sequence of data sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of all available and relevant information / validated methods requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All available and relevant information must be considered when conducting classifications; all classifications must be based on data generated using internationally validated and accepted methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA incorporated Rev. 8 language clarifying the obligation to consider all relevant information. This includes relying on internationally validated and accepted methods for data generation. OSHA moved some of its originally proposed sequencing text into alignment with Rev. 8's language that carries this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: In vitro/ex vivo and non-test methods acceptance and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA added paragraphs (A.2.2.3 on in vitro/ex vivo data and A.2.2.6 on non-test methods) providing information on classification based on in vitro/ex vivo data and non-test methods, along with applicability domain limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA expanded Appendix A to include these data streams to increase use of non-animal methods (consistent with Rev. 8). It also notes limitations and applicability domains; OSHA anticipates updating guidance products (including tables from Rev. 8) to provide further operational detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification criteria for skin corrosion (Table A.2.1 and A.2.2.2.1 series)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appendix A.2 (Table A.2.1 and paragraphs A.2.2.2.1, A.2.2.2.1.1, A.2.2.2.1.2) provide classification information and criteria for skin corrosion, including sub-categories 1A/1B/1C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA aligned these criteria with Rev. 8. The text organizes when to use subcategories and clarifies use of standard human and animal data, and test-derived thresholds. OSHA did not change substance-level classification criteria in essence, but changed wording/numbering and added guidance paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling variability in animal irritant responses (A.2.2.2.2.4 change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers should designate a substance as an irritant when at least one of three test animals show a very elevated mean score according to the test method used throughout the study, including lesions persisting at the end of an observation period of normally 14 days; other irritant responses should also fulfill the same criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA changed wording from “might”/“could” to “should” to clarify that classifiers should act when such variability is observed. OSHA believes guidance and examples provided elsewhere (Document ID 0008) give detailed rationale on applying classification principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin irritation Category 2 animal criterion (Table A.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The HCS skin irritation classification criteria align with the GHS reference tests where irritant responses are present in two of three tested animals for Category 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cal/OSHA questioned why two animals are required; OSHA responded that these criteria align with the GHS and any changes would be beyond the scope of this rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixtures: apply tiered approach and in vitro applicability (A.2.3.1.1–1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For mixtures, the tiered approach specified in Figure A.2.1 must be taken into account when evaluating mixtures. Paragraph A.2.3.1.2 provides information on using in vitro/ex vivo data and limitations regarding applicability domains. A.2.3.1.3 indicates that if no other data exist besides pH, extreme pH (pH ≤2 or pH ≥11.5) is sufficient to classify the mixture as corrosive unless acid/alkaline reserve suggests otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA added explicit text to require the tiered approach for mixtures and to clarify when pH alone is sufficient. If acid/alkaline reserve suggests non-corrosivity despite extreme pH, other data are needed to confirm. OSHA will provide more guidance on buffering capacity/acid–alkaline reserve in compliance assistance materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixtures classification concentration note to Table A.2.3 (cutoff/concentration triggers)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA finalized a note to Table A.2.3 describing the “Concentration of ingredients of a mixture classified as skin Category 1 or 2 that would trigger classification of the mixture as hazardous to skin (Category 1 or 2).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The note was finalized largely as proposed but edited to align with Rev. 8 (removing the phrase “data are available and”). This note is intended to provide useful information for classifiers about how ingredient concentrations trigger mixture classification, including sub-categorization where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buffering capacity / acid–alkaline reserve consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA recognizes the need to consider buffering capacity (acid/alkaline reserve) when pH is extreme and to determine whether a mixture is corrosive despite extreme pH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cal/OSHA noted inconsistent use and lack of definition; OSHA intends to update compliance assistance products and anticipates providing further guidance on acid/alkaline reserve (buffering capacity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eye damage tiering and footnote changes (Figure A.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Figure A.3.1 adopts a tiered evaluation for serious eye damage/eye irritation similar to skin: existing human data, existing animal data, in vitro data, then other sources. OSHA proposed footnote edits including: (a) expert judgment when interpreting animal data; (b) inclusion of OECD TG 460 (Fluorescein leakage) as an example of a validated test; (c) clarification that all available information must be considered (change 'should' to 'must'); and (d) negative results from applicable scientifically validated in vitro tests are considered in the total weight of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA finalized these footnote updates to clarify evaluator responsibilities and the role of validated in vitro tests. The agency also noted there are currently no validated in vitro tests for identifying eye irritation (as distinct from severe eye damage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronounced variability in animal responses must be considered (A.3.2.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is pronounced variability among animal responses, that information must be taken into account when determining classification (changed from 'may' to 'must').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksafe and Cal/OSHA raised concerns that 'may' permitted withholding evidence; OSHA agreed and revised the provision to mandate consideration of pronounced variability to clarify mandatory elements of Appendix A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference against conducting new animal tests (A.3.3.6 / A.3.2.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA indicates a preference for not conducting new animal tests and provides guidance on using the tiered approach and weight-of-evidence decisions to minimize new animal testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA reorganized prior paragraphs to provide guidance encouraging use of existing human/animal/in vitro data and other sources before resorting to new animal testing. No comments were received opposing this preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant-ingredient threshold for additivity in mixtures (1% rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: When using the additivity approach for mixtures (e.g., for Category 3 ingredients or aspiration hazard), the “relevant ingredients” are those present in concentrations ≥ one percent (w/w for solids, liquids, dusts, mists, and vapors and v/v for gases), unless there is reason to suspect that an ingredient present at <1% is still relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA proposed and finalized this numeric threshold (A.8.3.4.6 and A.10.3.3.1) to clarify which ingredients to include in additivity calculations. The proposal aligns with Rev. 7 and received no objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carcinogen classification cross-reference to 29 CFR 1910 subpart Z
rubrics_metrics.description: When OSHA has identified a chemical as a carcinogen in 29 CFR part 1910, subpart Z, that chemical must be classified as a carcinogen for purposes of the HCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA intended to retain the citation to 29 CFR part 1910, subpart Z (correcting an error in the NPRM that used 'this section subpart'). Commenters asked to allow authoritative organizations' listings (NTP, IARC, EPA) to mandate classification; OSHA declined changes outside the rulemaking scope but notes guidance (Appendix F) on mapping NTP/IARC listings to HCS classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Germ cell mutagenicity: definition and validated methods update
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA added a definition for germ cell mutagenicity in A.5.1.1 and proposed to update A.5.4 'Examples of scientifically validated test methods' by deleting the Mouse spot test (OECD 484) as it was deleted by the OECD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deletion of OECD 484 aligns Appendix A with Rev. 7 and contemporary scientific practice; classifiers should use the current list of validated methods when performing weight-of-evidence classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproductive toxicity—effects on or via lactation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA revised Figure A.7.1(b) to distinguish two separate effects captured by the lactation category: (1) substances that can interfere with lactation and (2) substances and their metabolites that may be transmitted through breast milk to children in amounts sufficient to cause concern. OSHA deleted the phrase 'hazardous to breastfed babies' and modified the third sentence to read: 'Classification for effects via lactation shall be assigned on the basis of:'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These edits clarify application of criteria without changing which substances are classified as reproductive toxicants. OSHA also added OECD TG 443 (Extended One Generation Reproductive Toxicity Study) to the list of acceptable test methods and corrected table heading wording to avoid suggesting additivity where not intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: STOT-SE and STOT-RE definitions and scope clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: STOT-SE refers to specific, non-lethal toxic effects on target organs after a single exposure; STOT-RE refers to specific toxic effects after repeated exposure. Each excludes effects addressed in other Appendix A sections (A.1–A.7 and A.10) and references the other where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA clarified that significant health effects that can impair function, reversible or irreversible, immediate or delayed, are included under STOT categories when not covered elsewhere. This separation clarifies classification routing between single and repeated exposure categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology consistency: replace 'toxicity category' with 'hazard category'
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed to delete the term 'toxicity category' and replace it with 'hazard category' in various places to ensure consistent use and align with Rev. 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes apply to A.0.5, A.1, A.3, A.8, A.9, A.10 and other places; no comments were received on this terminology harmonization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory language — converting 'should' to 'must' where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA updated several provisions in Appendix A to make clear that those provisions are mandatory (e.g., changing 'should' to 'must' in paragraph A.3.4.3.3 regarding cut-off values/concentrations in Table A.3.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intent is to clarify which elements are mandatory for classifiers (for example, cut-off concentrations used to determine if a mixture must be classified as seriously damaging to the eye or an eye irritant). OSHA made such changes where they align with the editorial and clarifying nature of the update.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration-bridging/principles corrections (include Appendix A.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA corrected omissions in the 2012 HCS by adding Appendix A.4 (respiratory or skin sensitization) to the list of health hazards referenced in concentration-of-mixtures and interpolation/bridging paragraphs (A.0.5.1.3 and A.0.5.1.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are corrections to ensure that concentration-of-mixtures bridging principles and interpolation within one category apply to respiratory and skin sensitization, aligning the text with intended policy.
